query: Which material can be used for improve the magnetocaloric properties, and why?

generation.hypothesis: An as‐cast FeCoNiTi high‐entropy alloy whose processing is tuned to promote a dominant fcc phase with enhanced Ti-induced antiferromagnetic coupling will show larger magnetic entropy changes (i.e. improved magnetocaloric effect) near its magnetic transitions.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast, polycrystalline FeCoNiTi high‐entropy alloy containing an fcc phase and minor secondary phases.
generation.intervention: Optimize the alloy’s composition (e.g., slightly increase or fine-tune the Ti content) and processing conditions to favor a dominant fcc phase with controlled chemical short-range order.
generation.conditions: Magnetic measurements performed over a broad temperature range (e.g. 50 K up to above 1000 K) under applied magnetic fields to capture the effects near the multiple ferromagnetic transitions.
generation.structural_mediator: The fcc phase whose local chemical environment (including Ti-induced antiferromagnetic coupling) tunes the saturation magnetization and magnetocrystalline anisotropy.
generation.mechanism: Ti atoms tend to couple antiferromagnetically with Fe, Co, and Ni. This lowers the saturation magnetization and increases magnetocrystalline anisotropy, which is correlated with a high coercive field. By tuning these magnetic interactions, the multiple ferromagnetic transitions of the alloy can be shifted or sharpened, thereby increasing the magnetic entropy change that is key to the magnetocaloric effect.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline as‐cast FeCoNiTi alloy, the optimized material will exhibit a larger magnetic entropy change at one or more of its magnetic transitions (e.g. around the 168 K or 1084 K transitions), indicating an improved magnetocaloric performance.
generation.baseline: Standard as‐cast FeCoNiTi high‐entropy alloy that shows three distinct ferromagnetic transitions (at approximately 1084 K, 214 K, and 168 K) with moderate coercive fields (around 489–667 Oe) and typical saturation magnetization.
generation.boundary: The enhancement is expected only when the processing yields a high fraction of the fcc phase and the Ti concentration is tuned within a window that favors antiferromagnetic interactions without inducing excessive phase instability or degrading ductility.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative link between slight Ti content adjustments, phase fraction control, and the resulting increase in magnetic entropy change is not yet established and requires systematic experimental investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of FeCoNiTi high‐entropy alloy samples with systematically varied Ti content and processing conditions aimed at increasing the fcc-phase fraction. Measure their magnetization as a function of temperature under applied magnetic fields and calculate the magnetic entropy change (ΔS_M) near the transition temperatures. Compare the ΔS_M of the modified alloys with that of the baseline composition.
measurements: Magnetization vs. Temperature curves at multiple applied fields
Calculation of magnetic entropy change (ΔS_M) via Maxwell relations
Phase analysis (XRD, SEM) to quantify fcc-phase fraction and chemical ordering
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the optimized alloys do not show a statistically significant (e.g., greater than 10%) increase in ΔS_M near at least one magnetic transition compared to the baseline alloy, or if no clear correlation is found between Ti tuning/fcc-phase fraction and enhanced magnetocaloric effect, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Paper card. Question: What are the magnetic properties of the as-cast high-entropy alloy FeCoNiTi, specifically regarding the origin of its multiple ferromagnetic transitions and the mechanism behind the high coercive field observed in the fcc phase?. System: FeCoNiTi (equiatomic Fe:Co:Ni:Ti = 1:1:1:1) and a C14-dominant variant Fe27Co27Ni17Ti29. Processing: Arc melting of elemental chips/wires (99.9% purity) in an Ar atmosphere on a water-cooled Cu hearth followed by rapid quenching to produce as-cast polycrystalline samples. Test conditions: DC magnetization measured from 50 to 1150 K under 100 Oe; Isothermal magnetization curves at 50, 100, 200, 300, and 400 K; Electronic structure calculations using CPA with PBE potential.
